Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PA Liberal Democrats Lib Dems propose big tech levy to fund £250m online crime agency Proposal one of many at conference responding to concern voters unaware of party’s policies or what it stands for Peter Walker and Alexandra Topping Sun 20 Sep 2026 17.30 EDT First published on Sun 20 Sep 2026 12.09 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The Liberal Democrats say they will tax big tech to finance a new online crime agency, as they try to address concerns that not enough voters know what the party stands for. The plan, to be announced at the party conference on Monday by the Lib Dems’ home affairs spokesperson, Max Wilkinson, would create a new Online Crime Agency focused on offences including child sexual abuse material, trafficking in drugs and weapons, and deepfake AI-generated pornographic images. The planned budget of £250m a year would be paid for by an “online crime levy” on large AI and technology companies. Wilkinson is to tell the conference it is “time they picked up the bill” for offences they had enabled. Ed Davey, the party leader, on Sunday set out a proposal to cut fuel duty by 10p a litre for a fixed three-month period, as well as reducing the bus fare cap from £3 to £1 and other transport-related cost of living policies. The party is increasingly concerned that, although it won its best election result in a century in 2024, it does not have a distinctive enough message to reach voters in an increasingly fragmented and noisy political landscape. Polling conducted to coincide with the conference in Brighton, released on Sunday, showed Lib Dem policies are less well known than those of Restore Britain, which launched as a political party only in February and has one MP – Rupert Lowe – compared with the Lib Dems’ 71. The research by More in Common, which was presented at the conference, showed widespread uncertainty among voters about what the Lib Dems stood for. Just 39% said they had an idea, lower than for every other major party, including Restore Britain, which was formed by Lowe after he split from Reform UK . Other parts of the research showed just 16% of voters said they had heard from the Lib Dems in recent months, against 66% for Reform, while 3% said they had seen Davey on social media, compared with 20% for the Reform leader, Nigel Farage. In a round of media interviews on Sunday morning, Davey pushed back against the idea that the Lib Dems, who are static in national polling at about 12%, risked being forgotten in the political conversation amid the rise in prominence of Reform and the Greens. His party, Davey insisted, was making a genuine difference, and not just generating coverage without substance. “I’m talking about real change, not just talking about the bubbles,” he told the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg show. “We have been winning council elections for eight years in a row. That has never happened before – it’s the most successful period that we’ve had.” While there is no talk among Lib Dem MPs about a challenge to Davey, some say they are frustrated the party’s message is too vague and its support too reliant on tactical voting in a limited number of places, mainly in the south of England. One Lib Dem MP told a conference fringe event, at which More in Common’s findings were presented, that the party needed to expand the geographical and social range of its influence. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion Ed Davey takes aim at Reform and Elon Musk as Lib Dem conference begins Read more “If we want to be a party of government, then we need to have a message for the whole country, not just parts of it,” said Tom Gordon, the MP for Harrogate and Knaresborough, one of just four Lib Dem-held seats in the north of England, against 58 in the south. Party figures see the conference as a chance to set out a more coherent and striking policy platform, including on the economy and immigration. But there is worry among some MPs that the problem is wider. “We already have quite a lot of policies, if people look at them,” one said. “It’s less about what you get if you vote Lib Dem than why you should – about what we represent. And people don’t really know that.” One longtime party activist said: “The voters only seem to properly notice us once every four years, when there’s an election. It’s a bit like being curling at the Winter Olympics – the rest of the time we’re forgotten. "The Lithuanian parliament plans to adopt a constitutional amendment this winter and remove the provision banning weapons of mass destruction on its territory from the country's basic law. This will require extending the autumn parliamentary session, which begins on Thursday," Olekas was quoted by the broadcaster LRT as saying. He added that the autumn session will have to be extended until January 13, 2027 so that the parliament can adopt this particular article of the constitution. Olekas said earlier that the provision of Article 137 of Lithuania's basic law, which rules out the deployment of nuclear weapons in the republic, no longer corresponds to geopolitical reality. In early July, the parliament approved an amendment to this article after the draft was presented. To amend Lithuania's constitution, at least 94 of the 141 parliamentarians must vote in favor twice, with a three-month interval between votes. © Sputnik

Skip next section Why have the Berlin exploratory talks broken down within a week? 10/13/2026 October 13, 2026 Why have the Berlin exploratory talks broken down within a week? Mark Hallam The breakdown in the exploratory talks can be traced back to concerns about the often highly critical stance on Israel adopted by some members of the Left Party , coupled with criticism of the appearance of a figure linked to organized crime at an election night party. The Left scored well with parts of Berlin's population, not least the young and communities with more people of migrant backgrounds, with an unusually stern line on Israeli wars in Gaza and elsewhere in the Middle East by the often muted standards of German politics. But comments from its more outspoken members and controversies like an organized crime boss attending an election-night after-party led to questions — particularly in some newspapers and from the conservative Christian Democrats — about whether center-left parties could work under the Left's leadership. In a bid to settle this, the Greens, SPD and Left drafted a joint statement on antisemitism, Israel's right to exist and maintaining a distance from organized crime before starting their talks. But the text subsequently faced criticism from within the Left's own ranks. On Tuesday, as 44 Left Party members of the new Berlin parliament met, they instead signed off on a different text more closely aligned to the party's past internal position papers. "We stand by Israel's right to exist and for equal rights for all people in Israel. Equally we stand by Palestine's right to exist and for equal rights for all people in Palestine," the Left Party's text read. Among other things, this omits a reference in the joint text to Israel's right to exist being "non-negotiable," and to listing potential sanctions for transgressions potentially extending as far as being ejected from the party. The CDU — which emerged as the second-largest party in the vote, well adrift of the Left on 18.8% — argue that the SPD and Greens should negotiate a coalition government with them instead. Chancellor Merz had also weighed into the discussion, saying that the allegations of impropriety facing the Left Party cannot be "dismissed with a piece of paper." In the meantime, the party's state lawmakers appear to have disavowed that piece of paper anyway. What's behind the rising polarization in German politics? The two parties' lead candidates from the state elections, Werner Graf of the Greens and Steffen Krach of the SPD, announced the move in a joint statement on Tuesday evening. They referred to Left Party meetings earlier in the day in which party members signed a statement on handling antisemitism and on Israel's right to exist , but using a text that differed from a statement the three parties had jointly agreed to when opening the negotiations. "We have taken note that the Left Party have reached a different arrangement within their own party," Graf and Krach's statement said. However, the SPD and Greens also made clear that they were not closing the door on the Left Party entirely. "This means that at this point we have to interrupt the coalition negotiations, so as to evaluate whether or not our agreement from last week still stands," they wrote. "We expect the Left Party to make clear to us to what extent they take the agreements they made seriously and intend to implement them." The Left Party emerged as the largest party Berlin's close-fought election last month, claiming just under 26% of the vote, faring particularly well with young voters . The Greens won just over 14% and the SPD just over 12% — meaning that the three left-leaning parties would command a slim majority if combined.
